items.title: Level 3: Delivering at Pace in everyday examples
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Delivering at Pace is about getting work done reliably and on time. At Administrative Officer level it means that you understand what you are responsible for, plan your tasks, put the most urgent ones first, keep going when things are hard, and ask for help early if you are going to miss a deadline. Panels do not expect a dramatic story. A good example might be clearing a backlog of post before a deadline, finishing coursework while caring for a relative, or covering extra shifts in a busy shop. What matters is how you organised yourself. Did you make a list? Did you decide what had to be done first, and why? Did you tell the right people when something slipped? Did you check your work before handing it in, so you did not have to redo it? Strong answers also explain how you kept your energy up, for instance by breaking a large job into small steps. Be careful not to describe a pace that costs quality. Rushing and making mistakes is not delivering well. The best examples show speed and accuracy together. A question might be 'Tell us about a time you had to complete a task to a tight deadline.' Begin with the deadline and the task, spend most of the time on your planning and actions, and finish with what was delivered, when, and what the people relying on you said or did.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes clearing a backlog of post before a deadline. What is the panel mainly looking for in the answer?

options.text: How many colleagues were helping them
How much post there was in total
How long the backlog had been building
How they planned and prioritised the work

questions.hint: The panel scores your planning and prioritising, not the amount of post.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest sign of good planning in a deadline example?

options.text: Waiting until the last day to see how much was left
Asking a colleague to choose the order each time
Starting at the first item and working through in order
Deciding what was most urgent and doing that first

questions.hint: Putting urgent work first shows planning.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'I rushed the forms and a few had mistakes, but they were in on time.' Why is this a weak example?

options.text: The candidate should have asked a colleague to help
The candidate should have used 'we' instead of 'I'
Speed has cost accuracy, so quality has suffered
The forms were handed in before the deadline had passed

questions.hint: Delivering well means both speed and accuracy.

questions.prompt: What is the best thing to do if you realise you will miss a deadline?

options.text: Wait to see if the deadline is extended before saying anything
Hand in what you have without mentioning the gap
Work through the night and hand in work that is rough
Tell the right person early and explain what you can deliver

questions.hint: Raising problems early is part of delivering at pace.

questions.prompt: Which small habit helps you deliver on time?

options.text: Waiting for reminders from your manager before you start
Keeping the whole task in your head instead of writing lists
Doing the easiest tasks first and the hardest ones last
Breaking a large job into smaller steps

questions.hint: Small steps make a big job manageable.

questions.prompt: A panel asks 'Tell us about a time you completed a task to a tight deadline.' What belongs at the start of your answer?

options.text: A long history of the organisation you worked for
A description of what you would do differently now
A short account of the deadline and the task
A list of every person involved in the project

questions.hint: Begin briefly with the deadline and the task.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows resilience under pressure?

options.text: Passing a difficult task to someone else
Finishing coursework while caring for a relative
Handing in an easy task a day early
Starting a deadline task again after missing it

questions.hint: Keeping going in difficult circumstances shows resilience.

questions.prompt: What should the end of a good Delivering at Pace answer include?

options.text: A promise to work faster in future than you did then
An apology for any stress the deadline caused others
What was delivered, when, and how people responded
The names of all the colleagues who were around at the time

questions.hint: The result shows what was delivered and its effect.

questions.prompt: Why do panels like to hear that you checked your work before handing it in?

options.text: It shows you aim for accuracy as well as speed
It shows you can slow a process down on purpose
It shows you did not trust your colleagues' work
It proves you had a lot of spare time that day

questions.hint: Checking prevents rework.

questions.prompt: Why do panels not expect a dramatic story for this behaviour?

options.text: Dramatic stories are nearly always exaggerated
Only very serious problems can be scored by a panel
Dramatic stories are not allowed in Civil Service interviews
Ordinary examples can show planning and persistence well

questions.hint: Everyday examples with clear planning are enough.

items.title: Level 3: Managing a Quality Service in everyday examples
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Managing a Quality Service is about giving people the service they need, accurately and fairly, and following the right processes. At Administrative Officer level it often means understanding who is relying on your work, checking details carefully, following procedures, keeping records up to date, and speaking up when something is not right. In the Civil Service the people who use a service may be members of the public, other departments or colleagues. A good example could come from a shop, a care setting, a school office or a call centre. For instance: you noticed that a form was being returned because the same box was often left blank, so you added a reminder to the guidance and the number of returned forms fell. That shows noticing a problem, taking a small action and checking the result. Panels also like examples that show you treated people fairly and respectfully, especially when someone was upset or confused. Another strong sign is following a process even when it was tempting to take a shortcut, and explaining why the process matters, such as protecting personal data. Accuracy is important in many AO jobs because mistakes can affect a person's payment or a decision about their case. If you made a mistake, the panel is interested in how you put it right and what you changed so it would not happen again. Ending with what you learned shows maturity.

questions.prompt: Who might be the 'users' of a service in the Civil Service?

options.text: Only the ministers who oversee the department
Only the people who pay a fee for the service
Only the people who work in the same office as you
Members of the public, other departments or colleagues

questions.hint: Service users can be the public or colleagues.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Completing every task as fast as you possibly can without stopping to check
Telling a manager that a task is too hard for you to finish alone
Doing every task the same way every time so that nothing is missed
Noticing a box was often left blank on a form and adding a reminder

questions.hint: Spotting a recurring problem and fixing it shows quality management.

questions.prompt: What is a strong sign of caring about quality in an example?

options.text: Following the process even when a shortcut was tempting
Leaving the checking to whoever handles it next
Skipping checks when the work seemed simple enough
Changing the process without telling anyone about it

questions.hint: Following the process shows care for quality.

questions.prompt: Why does following a process matter in many AO jobs?

options.text: It protects people's information and keeps treatment fair
It gives you a reason to avoid helping customers
It keeps work slow enough for other teams to catch up
It is only needed when a manager is watching you

questions.hint: Processes protect data and fairness.

questions.prompt: A candidate admits making a mistake with a customer's details. What should the answer focus on?

options.text: How they put it right and what they changed afterwards
Who else might have made the same mistake in the team
Why the mistake was not really their fault
How rarely mistakes of that kind happen

questions.hint: The panel wants to see correction and learning.

questions.prompt: Which of these shows treating an upset customer fairly?

options.text: Explaining the rules once and ending the conversation
Passing them quickly to a colleague without any explanation
Agreeing with everything they say so that they calm down
Letting them explain, then clearly explaining the next steps

questions.hint: Listening and explaining shows respect.

questions.prompt: Why is accuracy so important in many AO jobs?

options.text: Mistakes can affect a person's payment or a decision
Accurate work is never checked by anyone else
Panels give extra marks for neat handwriting on forms
Accurate work is quicker and so counts for more marks

questions.hint: Errors can have real consequences for people.

questions.prompt: How could a candidate show they checked the result of a change?

options.text: They counted how many forms were returned afterwards
They assumed it had worked because it made sense
They told their manager that the change was a good idea
They waited to see whether anyone complained

questions.hint: Checking results provides evidence.

questions.prompt: Which setting could give a good example for this behaviour?

options.text: Only a bank or other financial company
A shop, school office, care setting or call centre
Only a government office or another public body
Only a large company with a formal training scheme

questions.hint: Any setting where you served people can work.

questions.prompt: What does finishing with what you learned show?

options.text: That you have never made a mistake
That the story was prepared with a coach
That the panel need not ask any more questions
Maturity and a willingness to improve

questions.hint: Reflection shows maturity.

items.title: Level 3: Working Together in everyday examples
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Working Together is one of the most common behaviours at Administrative Officer level. The Civil Service wants people who build good relationships, share information, support others and are open to different views. Everyday examples are perfect. You might have helped a new colleague learn a system, shared the workload when a teammate was off sick, or worked with a group at college. A strong example does not mean you got on with everyone. Often the best stories involve a small difficulty, such as two people who disagreed about the best way to do a job, or a team member who was not pulling their weight. What matters is how you handled it. Did you talk to the person privately and respectfully? Did you try to understand their point of view before giving yours? Did you find a compromise or agree a plan? Did you keep helping the team, even though it was not part of your own job? Be honest about your own part, and avoid naming and blaming. A story that shows you taking the initiative to include a quiet colleague, or sharing credit with the team afterwards, is attractive to panels. At the same time, the panel is scoring you, so use 'I' for your actions and say 'we' only when you describe the team's result. A balanced answer shows what you did for the team, and what the team achieved because of it.

questions.prompt: A story where you handled a small difficulty in a team is usually better than which alternative?

options.text: A story with very detailed background
A story where everyone agreed and nothing was difficult
A story from the last week
A story about a team you led

questions.hint: How you handle a difficulty shows more than a smooth story.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows consideration when you disagree with a colleague?

options.text: Doing the task your own way and informing them later
Talking to them privately and listening to their view first
Asking the manager to decide before speaking to them
Telling the rest of the team about the disagreement

questions.hint: Understanding their view first shows respect.

questions.prompt: A teammate was not pulling their weight. Which approach best fits the behaviour?

options.text: Doing their work in silence and keeping quiet about it
Telling the rest of the team that the work was unequal
Speaking to them respectfully to find out what was wrong
Reporting them to the manager at the first sign of delay

questions.hint: A respectful conversation shows maturity.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid naming and blaming in your answer?

options.text: It suggests you cannot work well with other people
Names cannot be used in a STAR answer
It makes the story too short to be scored properly
Panels forbid candidates from mentioning other people

questions.hint: Blame weakens a Working Together answer.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of taking the initiative to include others?

options.text: Inviting a quiet colleague to share their ideas in a meeting
Speaking for the quiet colleague so they are not put on the spot
Giving the quiet colleague extra tasks to build confidence
Leaving the quiet colleague alone to avoid awkwardness

questions.hint: Including quieter colleagues shows team spirit.

questions.prompt: How should you use 'I' and 'we' in a team story?

options.text: 'I' for the result only, and 'we' for the actions
'We' throughout, to sound modest and team-minded
'I' for your actions, 'we' for the team's result
'They' for every action taken by the team

questions.hint: The panel is scoring you, so say what you did.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good example of Working Together?

options.text: Working alone to avoid slowing anyone else down
Taking the most interesting tasks to keep things moving
Sharing the workload when a teammate was off sick
Waiting to be asked before offering to help

questions.hint: Helping out shows teamwork.

questions.prompt: Why is sharing credit with the team afterwards attractive to panels?

options.text: It is required in every answer by the Civil Service Code
It shows you value other people's contributions
It means you can skip describing the result
It makes your own part in the work look bigger

questions.hint: Sharing credit builds relationships.

questions.prompt: A candidate helped a new colleague learn a system. What would strengthen the example?

options.text: Saying that the colleague had been slow to learn
Saying how they explained it and how the colleague got on
Saying how long the system has been in use
Saying that the manager approved of the system

questions.hint: Detail about actions and result strengthens it.

questions.prompt: Which source could provide a good Working Together story?

options.text: A college group project
Only a story told to you by another person
Only a team sport played at a high level
Only a full-time paid job in an office

questions.hint: Group work at college is a valid source.

items.title: Level 3: Communicating and Influencing in everyday examples
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Communicating and Influencing is about getting your message across and listening to others. For Administrative Officer jobs it often means writing clear emails and letters, answering the phone politely, explaining a process to someone who does not know it, and listening before you respond. Good examples are easy to find. You may have calmed a worried customer, explained a rota change to colleagues, written a notice for a club or helped a relative to understand a letter from a government service. A strong answer shows that you thought about the other person. Who were they? What did they already know? What did they need? Perhaps you used plain words instead of jargon, or you wrote the key date at the top of the message. Perhaps you checked that they had understood by asking them to say it back in their own words. Influencing in this context does not mean pushing people. It means explaining your reasons honestly so that someone can agree or give their view. In written work, accuracy and tone matter: a short, polite, well-organised email is often better than a long one. For phone and face-to-face work, tone of voice and listening are as important as the words. If your example is about a hard conversation, say how you kept calm and respectful, and what you did to reach an outcome. Do not claim your message was perfect. Mention anything you changed afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an everyday example of Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Reading a long document on your own
Doing your own work without telling anyone about it
Waiting for instructions before acting
Explaining a rota change to colleagues

questions.hint: Explaining a change clearly shows communication.

questions.prompt: What question should you ask yourself when planning how to explain something?

options.text: How can I use the most precise technical words?
How quickly can I get through it?
How many other people can I copy in?
What does this person already know and need?

questions.hint: Thinking about the listener shapes clear communication.

questions.prompt: Why might a candidate put the key date at the top of an email?

options.text: So the details further down can be left out
So the email looks longer and more thorough
So the manager is impressed by the layout
So the reader sees the most important point first

questions.hint: Putting key information first helps the reader.

questions.prompt: How could you check that someone understood a process?

options.text: Ask whether they have any questions in general
Give them a longer written document to read
Repeat the whole process a little more slowly
Ask them to say it back in their own words

questions.hint: Asking them to say it back checks understanding.

questions.prompt: What does 'influencing' mean in an AO context?

options.text: Explaining your reasons honestly so others can agree or disagree
Making sure that your own idea is the one chosen
Avoiding any kind of disagreement with others
Persuading people to accept your decision with firm arguments

questions.hint: Influencing is honest explanation, not pressure.

questions.prompt: Which is usually better in written work?

options.text: A quick message with no greeting or sign-off
A short, polite and well-organised email
An email that states strong opinions clearly
A long email that covers every possible detail

questions.hint: Short, clear emails are often better.

questions.prompt: In a phone call with a worried customer, what matters as much as the words?

options.text: How many times you say the customer's name
The speed at which you type notes during the call
The type of phone and headset you are using
Your tone of voice and how well you listen

questions.hint: Tone and listening matter on the phone.

questions.prompt: If your example is about a hard conversation, what should you explain?

options.text: Who else was present when it took place
How you stayed calm and respectful and reached an outcome
Why the other person was in the wrong
How quickly the conversation was over

questions.hint: The panel wants to see calm, respectful handling.

questions.prompt: Why should you mention anything you changed afterwards?

options.text: It makes the example longer and more detailed
It shows learning and honesty about the first attempt
It shows the first attempt had failed completely
It lets you avoid describing the main result

questions.hint: Reflection shows maturity.

questions.prompt: Which source could give a good Communicating example?

options.text: Reading an email from a stranger about work
Helping a relative understand a government letter
Watching a recorded talk on how to communicate well
Reading a book about influence and persuasion

questions.hint: Helping someone understand is a real example.

items.title: Level 3: Developing Self and Others and learning from feedback
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Developing Self and Others is about taking responsibility for your own learning and helping others to improve. At Administrative Officer level, panels want to see that you ask for feedback, listen to it without getting defensive, and use it to do better. A good example might be asking a supervisor how to improve a report, learning a new computer system by practising in your own time, or showing a new starter how to use a till. Learning from mistakes is also welcome. Everybody makes them, and a clear account of what went wrong, what you did and how you changed your habits shows maturity. Developing others does not mean being a manager. It could be explaining a task to a friend at college or giving a colleague a tip that saved them time. A strong answer for this behaviour usually includes the following parts. First, what you wanted to improve and why. Second, what you did, such as practising, asking questions, finding a guide, taking a short course or watching someone more experienced. Third, how you checked that you had improved. Fourth, how you used the new skill. If you are talking about feedback, say what the other person said, what you felt and what you did. Being honest that you found some feedback hard to hear can make the answer more believable, as long as you show how you responded constructively.

questions.prompt: What is Developing Self and Others about?

options.text: Taking charge of other people's work so it is done correctly
Avoiding mistakes at all costs in front of your manager
Taking charge of your own learning and helping others
Waiting to be trained by someone more senior

questions.hint: The behaviour covers learning and helping others.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good example of taking responsibility for your own learning?

options.text: Asking a colleague to do the task for you
Practising a new computer system in your own time
Waiting for a manager to arrange formal training
Avoiding the system until it is compulsory

questions.hint: Self-directed practice shows responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of developing others at AO level?

options.text: Showing a new starter how to use a till
Carrying out an appraisal of your own manager
Setting yearly targets for a team of staff
Writing a training plan for a whole department

questions.hint: Showing someone how to do a task is developing others.

questions.prompt: What should your answer say about feedback you found hard to hear?

options.text: How you responded constructively and what you changed
That you set it aside and carried on as before
That the feedback was unfair and you explained why
That you argued your case until it was withdrawn

questions.hint: Constructive response is what matters.

questions.prompt: Why is a clear account of a mistake helpful in this behaviour?

options.text: It proves you rarely make mistakes of any kind
It shows maturity and how you changed your habits
It makes the answer shorter and easier to score
It moves the focus away from your own part

questions.hint: Learning from mistakes is welcome.

questions.prompt: Which part of a good answer shows that you improved?

options.text: How long you waited before you started
How you checked that you had got better
Who first suggested that you should learn it
Which book or course you chose

questions.hint: Checking progress shows improvement.

questions.prompt: What does a strong Developing Self answer usually say first?

options.text: What you thought of the feedback you got
What you wanted to improve and why
Who your manager was at the time
How long you had been in the job

questions.hint: Start with the aim.

questions.prompt: Does developing others require you to be a manager?

options.text: It counts only if it happens in a paid job with a manager
Anyone can help others, for example with a useful tip
Only senior managers can run a development plan
Only managers are able to develop other people

questions.hint: Anyone can help others learn.

questions.prompt: Which method of learning might an AO candidate sensibly mention?

options.text: Avoiding unfamiliar tasks until they are essential
Waiting until someone offers to teach you
Watching someone more experienced do the task
Memorising a long list of rules before starting

questions.hint: Watching and asking are valid learning methods.

questions.prompt: Why does admitting that feedback was hard to hear make an answer more believable?

options.text: It shows realistic feelings alongside a constructive response
It shows you do not like being corrected by managers
It shows that you disagreed with the feedback you got
It shows you rarely ask for feedback in future

questions.hint: Honesty adds credibility.

items.title: Level 3: Making Effective Decisions at entry level
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Making Effective Decisions is about using the information you have to choose a sensible course of action. At Administrative Officer level the focus is not on big policy choices. It is on everyday judgement. Good examples show that you understood the issue, gathered the facts you needed, thought about the options, chose one, and were ready to ask for guidance when a decision was beyond your authority. A typical example could be deciding how to deal with a customer's request that did not quite fit the rules. You might have checked the guidance, asked a colleague who had seen a similar case and then explained the next step to the customer. Another could be choosing between two tasks when both were urgent, by asking your manager which mattered more. Panels like to see you weighing up the choice and not simply guessing. They also like to see that you know the limits of your role. Not every decision is yours to make, and passing it on to the right person is a good decision too. Be careful with examples where you ignored the rules because you thought you knew better. That can look like a lack of respect for process. Explain why you made the choice, what evidence you used, how you felt about the risk, and what happened. If the decision turned out badly, say what you learned. The panel is interested in the quality of your thinking.

questions.prompt: At Administrative Officer level, what is Making Effective Decisions mainly about?

options.text: Making decisions without needing to check the rules
Making decisions as quickly as you possibly can
Making large decisions about policy for your department
Using the information you have to choose a sensible action

questions.hint: Everyday judgement based on information is the focus.

questions.prompt: A customer's request does not quite fit the rules. What is a sensible first step?

options.text: Say no straight away to keep things simple
Check the guidance and ask an experienced colleague
Pass the customer to another team without any explanation
Make an exception without telling anyone

questions.hint: Using guidance and colleagues is good judgement.

questions.prompt: Which shows good decision-making when two tasks are both urgent?

options.text: Choosing the one you find more interesting
Asking your manager which one matters more
Waiting until someone chases you for one of them
Doing both at the same time as best you can

questions.hint: Asking about priorities is sensible.

questions.prompt: Why is passing a decision to the right person sometimes a good decision?

options.text: It saves the panel from hearing a longer answer
It is always the quickest way to the right answer
Not every decision is yours to make
It shows you cannot make up your mind

questions.hint: Knowing your limits is part of good judgement.

questions.prompt: Why can an example where you ignored the rules look poor?

options.text: It shows you were working at too fast a pace
It can show a lack of respect for process
It shows you were being creative with the task
It shows strong leadership of a small team

questions.hint: Ignoring rules can suggest poor judgement.

questions.prompt: What should you say about the evidence behind your choice?

options.text: How confident you felt on the day
How long you spent thinking about it
What information you used and why
How many other people you told about it

questions.hint: Evidence shows the quality of thinking.

questions.prompt: If a decision turned out badly, what is the best thing to say?

options.text: What you learned from it
Who else was involved in making it
Why the decision was the right one at the time
That it was beyond your control

questions.hint: Learning is valued.

questions.prompt: Which of these shows you weighed up options?

options.text: Choosing the first option that came to mind
Going with the option you chose last time
Waiting to see which option most people chose
Comparing two ways of handling a request before choosing

questions.hint: Comparing options shows thought.

questions.prompt: What does the panel mainly score in a decision example?

options.text: The size of the decision you made
How quickly you reached a decision
The quality of your thinking
The outcome and nothing else

questions.hint: The panel scores your thinking, not just the result.

questions.prompt: Which source could provide a good decision-making example?

options.text: Deciding where to go on holiday with your family
Dealing with an unusual customer request at a till
Deciding what to order from a menu this week
Deciding how to spend a government budget this year

questions.hint: Everyday work decisions are suitable.

items.title: Level 3: Spotting what is missing in a STAR answer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: A good way to improve your answers is to listen for the missing part. Imagine a candidate says: 'I worked in a cafe. One morning the coffee machine broke and the queue got long. We managed to get everyone served and the boss was happy.' This answer gives the Situation, and a vague Result, but no Task and almost no Action. The panel cannot tell what the candidate personally did. A better answer would say: 'I was the only person on the till when the machine broke. My job was to keep customers calm while we fixed it. I told the queue what had happened and offered tea or cold drinks, I asked a colleague to phone the engineer, and I took payment by card for drinks we still could make. Within twenty minutes the queue was cleared and the manager thanked me.' Now the panel can see the Task, three Actions and a Result. Another common problem is a candidate who spends two minutes on the Situation, so there is little time for Action. A third is an answer that stops at the Action and never says what happened. A fourth is an answer that uses 'we' throughout. When you practise, ask a friend to listen and tell you which letter of STAR was missing or too thin. You can also record yourself and write down what you hear. Aim to improve one thing at a time: first make the Actions clear, then add the Result with a number or a reaction.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'The machine broke, the queue grew, and we got everyone served.' Which part of STAR is almost missing?

options.text: Situation, because it was not described at all
Result, because everyone was served
Action, because we do not know what they personally did
Task, because nothing had been set

questions.hint: The candidate does not say what they personally did.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the clearest Action statement?

options.text: 'We tried to deal with the problem together as a team.'
'The queue was told what had happened at the time.'
'Things were sorted out by the end of the morning.'
'I told the queue what happened and offered cold drinks.'

questions.hint: A specific 'I' statement is the clearest action.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with an answer that spends two minutes on the Situation?

options.text: The panel will not understand the situation
There is too little time left for the Action
The answer will be too short overall
The Result will become too long

questions.hint: Too much context squeezes out the evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with an answer that stops after the Action?

options.text: The panel does not know what happened as a result
The Action will not be clear enough to be scored
The Situation will have been left out of the answer
The answer will be too long for the time allowed

questions.hint: Results are needed to show effect.

questions.prompt: Why does using 'we' throughout weaken an answer?

options.text: It breaks the time limit for the question
It makes the answer too short to be scored
The panel cannot tell what you personally did
The panel dislikes any mention of teamwork

questions.hint: The panel can only score your actions.

questions.prompt: In the improved cafe answer, what is the Task?

options.text: Phoning the engineer about the machine
Taking payment by card for the drinks
Keeping customers calm while the machine was fixed
Serving cold drinks to the queue

questions.hint: The Task is the goal in the situation.

questions.prompt: A friend listens to your answer. What is the most useful thing to ask them?

options.text: How many minutes the answer lasted in total
Whether they enjoyed the story
Which letter of STAR was missing or thin
Whether you sounded confident enough

questions.hint: Identifying a weak part gives a clear target.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible way to improve an answer step by step?

options.text: Make the answer longer overall, then trim it
Make the Actions clear first, then add a strong Result
Learn the answer by heart, then adjust it
Add more background first, then the Actions

questions.hint: Improve one thing at a time.

questions.prompt: How could you strengthen a vague Result like 'the boss was happy'?

options.text: Remove it and end on the Action
Make it sound more positive
Move it to the start of the answer
Add a number or a clear reaction

questions.hint: Specific outcomes are more convincing.

questions.prompt: Why might recording yourself help?

options.text: It proves that you are ready for the interview
It shortens the answer by cutting the pauses
You can hear and write down what is missing
It replaces the need for any further practice

questions.hint: Listening back shows gaps.

items.title: Level 3: Strengths questions in practice
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Strengths questions often come in a quick run. You might be asked, 'Would you rather plan a task or get on with it?', 'What do you find easy that others find hard?' or 'How do you feel when you have to change plans?' Because there is little time, the best approach is to answer honestly and briefly, then add a short reason. For example: 'I would rather plan, because I like to know where I am heading, but I can change when I need to.' Notice that the answer shows a preference, gives a reason and shows flexibility. You do not need to pretend to like everything. Panels prefer authentic answers, and a job where you will be doing things you enjoy is better for you. It is also important not to describe a strength as the opposite of what the role needs. If the job is detailed administration, saying you hate paperwork is honest, but it suggests the job might not suit you. In that case it is worth thinking carefully before applying. Strengths questions may also ask what you did well recently or what you are proud of. Choose something real, say how you felt, and keep it short. Avoid long stories. Because the panel is watching for energy, speak with natural warmth. Smile if it feels right. Do not try to give the answer you think they want, as it usually shows. If you notice you have given a one-word answer, you can add a sentence of explanation.

options.text: With a long STAR example from a past job
With a single word and nothing else
Honestly and briefly, with a short reason
With the answer you think the panel prefers

questions.hint: A short honest answer with a reason works best.

options.text: A preference, a reason and some flexibility

questions.hint: It combines honesty with adaptability.

Authentic answers match the advert exactly

questions.hint: Authenticity helps both sides.

questions.hint: Honest self-awareness helps you choose the right job.

questions.hint: A short, real answer is best.

items.title: Level 3: The day of a video interview, step by step
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: On the day of a video interview, a simple routine keeps you calm. The evening before, check the time, the link and the contact number on your invitation. Charge your device, put your notes beside you, and lay out smart clothes. In the morning, eat a light breakfast and drink some water. Allow plenty of time to get ready, and finish any household tasks that might interrupt you. About thirty minutes before the start, switch off notifications, silence your phone, close other programs and set up your room: plain wall behind you, light on your face, camera at eye level. Put ID, a pen, paper and a glass of water within reach. Open the link about ten minutes before the start. Many panels use a waiting room, where you will stay until the host lets you in. Don't worry if you are kept waiting for a few minutes, as panels often run slightly late. When you are admitted, say a clear hello, check they can hear you, and wait to be introduced. During the interview, keep your notes brief. If the panel's picture freezes, tell them. If there is a loud noise outside, apologise briefly and carry on. When the questions end, ask your prepared question, thank them and wait until the host closes the meeting. Afterwards, close the call properly, take a walk or have a drink, and write a few notes about what you were asked while it is fresh.

questions.hint: A clear greeting and sound check starts well.

questions.hint: Notes help with later interviews and feedback.

questions.hint: Fewer interruptions mean a calmer interview.

items.title: Level 3: Handling difficult questions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Some questions feel tricky, but they are usually easier than they seem if you know the approach. 'Tell us about a time you made a mistake' is not a trap. The panel wants to see honesty and learning. Choose a small but real mistake, say what you did to put it right, and explain what you now do differently. Avoid answers that blame others or that claim you have never made one. 'What is your weakness?' is another common question, particularly in strengths-based interviews. Pick a real, minor weakness that you are working on, and show what you are doing about it. Avoid disguised strengths, such as 'I work too hard', which sound insincere. 'Tell us about a time you disagreed with someone' needs a story where you stayed respectful and reached a solution. 'Tell us about a time you failed' is similar to the mistake question. 'Why should we choose you?' asks you to link your skills to the job. Mention two or three relevant strengths, backed by a short example. If you are asked a question you do not understand, ask for clarification. If you do not have an example, be honest. Say, 'I haven't been in exactly that situation, but here is a similar one', or explain how you would approach it. What the panel wants to see is a calm, thoughtful person who can learn. Do not argue with a question or say it is unfair.

questions.prompt: What is the panel looking for in a question about a mistake?

options.text: Proof that you rarely make mistakes
A reason the mistake could not be avoided
Honesty and learning
A reason why other people were at fault

questions.hint: The question tests honesty and learning.

questions.prompt: Which type of mistake is a sensible choice for the answer?

options.text: One you heard about from a friend
A small but real one that you put right
A serious one that caused harm to others
One you invented to fit the question

questions.hint: A small, real mistake lets you show learning.

'I work too hard and find it hard to switch off.'

questions.hint: A real weakness plus action is believable.

options.text: Panels hear them often and see through them

They are against the rules of the interview

questions.hint: They avoid answering honestly.

questions.hint: Linking skills to the job is the aim.

questions.hint: Honesty with an alternative is acceptable.

options.text: Ask the panel to explain why it is being asked

Give a short answer and mention it is unfair

questions.hint: Arguing does not help.

How well you know the members of the panel
How much detail you can remember about the past
How fast you can speak under pressure

questions.hint: The panel looks for calm, thoughtful learners.

options.text: Wait in silence until they rephrase it
Ask for clarification
Answer the part you think you understood

questions.hint: Clarifying is perfectly acceptable.

items.title: Level 3: Making a good impression with the panel
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Panels form an impression from the moment you appear, though they are scoring the evidence you give, not your personality. Still, small things help you to come across well. On arrival, whether in person or online, be polite and friendly to everyone you meet, including receptionists. Greet the panel with a smile and a clear hello. If you are in a room, wait to be told where to sit. Sit upright but comfortably and keep your hands relaxed. Avoid folding your arms, which can look defensive, and avoid fidgeting with a pen. Speak at a steady pace and at a comfortable volume. Vary your tone so you don't sound flat. Show you are listening by looking at the person asking, nodding and not interrupting. When you answer, try to look at the person who asked, then include the others. If you make a mistake, correct it and move on. Be positive about previous jobs and colleagues. Avoid slang, swearing or too much casual language, but don't try to sound overly formal either. Be yourself. Dress smartly but comfortably, in clothes that you feel good in. There is no uniform. For an entry-level role, a clean shirt or blouse with smart trousers or a skirt is fine. If you are not sure about the dress code, it is better to be slightly smart than too casual. Finally, thank the panel on leaving.

Your choice of clothes
Your handwriting

questions.hint: Scores come from evidence against the criteria.

questions.hint: Natural but professional works best.

questions.hint: Slightly smart is the safer choice.

items.title: Level 3: Offers, checks and feedback
items.body: If the panel decides you did well, the recruitment team will contact you with an offer, usually by email or through Civil Service Jobs. Read it carefully, as it will set out the job title, grade, location, salary and the conditions that must be met. These conditions are the pre-employment checks. The most common are proof of identity and right to work, references from recent employers or other referees, and a basic criminal record check. Many roles also need the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, and some need higher security vetting, which takes longer. You may be asked to fill in forms and provide documents such as a passport or driving licence. Do this promptly, as delays can slow the start date. Remember that the offer is conditional until the checks are complete. Do not resign from your current job until the recruitment team confirms the offer is unconditional and you have an agreed start date. If you are offered a job, you can ask questions about it, for example about working patterns or the start date. If the offer is not what you expected, you may negotiate, though pay for most Civil Service grades is fixed within a range. If you do not get a job, the feedback can be very helpful. Ask for it politely, and use it for your next application. Remember that some candidates are held on a reserve list and might be offered a job later, so reply promptly if you are contacted.
